utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearance today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Gerard Dobbyn, and our Case Manager today is Indah Susanti.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning, Your Honours, for the Defence of Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, Aleksandar Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no housekeeping matters, could the witness be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, good morning to you, sir. Before Mr. Zecevic resumes his examination-in-chief, I remind you you are still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] good morning, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, what was your task when you were sent to Brcko in the beginning of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To carry out an inspection, supervision and to provide the indispensable assistance for the revitalisation of the police station in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Brcko, tell me what did you find at the police station, or rather the public security station Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I arrived in Brcko, after all this was my first encounter with that kind of an emergency, state of emergency. I arrived at some point in the afternoon. There was quite a destruction. Buildings were damaged. I was put up at a hotel, Brcko, to spend the night and early in the morning I went to the police station. At the police station I only saw the duty policeman and some persons who were coming into this police station, going out, I had no idea who these individuals were and what they were doing. I addressed the duty policeman, I introduced myself and I asked him to take me to the office of the chief of the public security station. In the hallway of that police station, I stayed for several hours until an individual came who introduced himself as the chief of the public security station. I think his name was Dragan Veselic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this Dragan Veselic, who introduced himself to you as the chief of the public security station, did he tell you who had appointed him to that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to answer that question given the time distance. However, it was my understanding at the time that the current authorities in Brcko had appointed him. Whether consent and approval had been received from the MUP or not I don't know, to this day. But it is certain that he was appointed by the then authorities of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This gentleman, Mr. Veselic, was he a member of the MUP before that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the MUP. As we talked it seemed to me that he was basically involved in politics and it was the Serb Democratic Party that had proposed him as a candidate for the chief of the public security station, so he was not a professional in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at 65 ter 182D1, tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, at the public security station of Brcko, did you organise a meeting to familiarise yourself with the situation there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I held my first meeting with Mr. Veselic on that very same day and I expressed my interest in all the police stations that the Brcko police station was facing. He familiarised me with the situation there and while I was waiting for him to receive me in his office, what I saw was that it was internal order that was their main problem. Let me explain this. I think that people enter that police station any way they wanted, they went to different offices, they took certain documents any which way they wanted to, primarily driving licences and traffic licences. So my primary objective was to overcome that situation first and foremost. Before the official meeting that we organised at the police station, I was the one who had requested that meeting, because at the time the police station, as far as I can remember, did not have a commander of the police station. There wasn't a deputy there either. I think there were two assistant commanders and that's how it all functioned. I said to Mr. Veselic what I thought and what my proposals were, namely, to focus first and foremost on getting the house in order and let us try to establish a standing practice, not to say a pre-war practice, not to allow persons with weapons to enter the police station. And most of them had long-barrelled weapons at that. And that they exercised their civic rights without being armed. As for that task, we needed a few very brave and courageous young men because our assessment was that there would be quite a few problems, that the people who were used to entering the police station in that way would try to go on doing so. We selected about ten young men and I held a meeting with them. In the meantime, we made a kind of document showing that weaponry had been taken away temporarily from a person, any kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you introduced this order in the house, if we can put it that way, this internal order within the public security station, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later we had a problem straightaway. Some paramilitary formation, I think they were Captain Dragan's men, they were led by a certain Rade. With their weapons and equipment, they tried to enter the building violently, these young men who were on duty there opposed that, and thankfully they emerged victorious. Fire-arms were not used in the process. So they emerged victorious and in a way people felt relieved after that and could work in the police station in a more normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Andan, when you came to the police station of Brcko, the public security station in Brcko, did they have an organised patrol service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problem was that they only had a duty service that was operating. All the police forces that they had at that point in time were at the front line. The army had carried out mobilisation of the police forces as well and took them to the front line. At that point in time apart from the duty service that had about five or six men and the chief and myself and two assistants, there weren't any other policemen at the police station, so they did not have a proper professional division into departments which is indispensable for the proper functioning of a police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please let us have a look at the document before us. These are minutes from the professional collegium of the Serbian SJB, held on the 2nd of June, 1992. Did you attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I attended the meeting. I was the one who initiated it. However, before this meeting something else happened that was very important for the Brcko police station. I asked Chief Veselic that we withdraw the active-duty policemen from the front line, and that withdraw some of the reserve police force so that we could properly start organising the work of the police station. With Mr. Veselic, I went to the command, the military command in Brcko, we presented our problem, and we were promised that as soon as possible, within a day or two, we would get some feedback, or rather, that about 150 to 170 policemen would be returned from the front lines, some of them active duty, others reserve. After that we opened this working meeting, the one that I had initiated. Our first task was to establish a structure of command in the police station in Brcko, before we started the official meeting, this working meeting of the structures of the police station, I gave general guide-lines to the chief of the police station as to how the meeting should be organised. With all due respect the man had never worked in police structures before, so I had to explain to him all the segments of work in a police station and to say what was the most important thing that had to be done in a police station so that it would start functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "start functioning" is it your view that the public security station in Brcko before that moment, that is to say the beginning of June when you arrived there, had not actually been functioning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is regular practice in the ministry that when one first arrives in a police station, one observes the entire situation as it is and then we send a report. This was done in peacetime and it was also done in war time, wherever possible. I think that I did that, and when I arrived in the police station, I observed the overall situation on the basis of my own information, I said that the police station in Brcko functioned until the bridges on the Sava river were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when was that approximately, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have that particular piece of information, you will know. I think it was sometime in the beginning of April 1992. After that all Serb, Croat and Muslim personnel had left the police station, at least to the best of my knowledge. However, according to what I learned during this inspection, the Muslims took log-books and registers from the police station and all the other necessary administrative papers. They took the seals as well and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I ask if there needs to be a clarification at line 8, it says, "all Serb, Croat, and Muslim personnel left". That sounds like it doesn't leave anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard this, didn't you, is that your knowledge, that no one stayed behind at the police station after the bridges were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Brcko police station very few Serb policemen remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you allow me, I would like to say that that situation prevailed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic, the clarification which the witness has just offered I confess confuses me somewhat in that the broad statement that he made initially which Mr. Hannis invited clarification on, the way it has been clarified leads me to question whether it was only Serb policemen who remained. Do you understand, Mr. Andan? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand what you are saying. I said that Serb, Croat, and Muslim policemen had left and that only a number of Serb policemen had stayed behind at the police station, so some policemen had stayed on at the police station in Brcko. I also said that the Muslims had left and that they took along part of the documentation and the registers and the seals. I don't know if we are understanding each other on this, only very few Serb policemen stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My question is whether of those who stayed behind, they were only Serbs. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the information that I received when I came to the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I put a follow-up question to the information that you have just offered in response to the Presiding Judge's question, namely, why would any Serb police officer leave the SJB of Brcko at that time, that is to say, after the bridges were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you a specific answer. I can just offer certain facts to you because of the shortage of personnel when I arrived there, as assigned by Mr. Stanisic to Brcko, and when we tried to constitute the ministry, or rather, the public security station, we did not have an adequate number of personnel who would provide the manpower for all the services required within the police station. When I asked where Serb personnel were, the answer I was given was that they had left as well and that they were most probably at their apartments and houses. Then I asked the chief to call each and every one of them individually to have them brought back to the police station because we needed professionals to carry out police work. I don't know whether they all responded, but most of them did return to the police station and we assigned them to certain jobs and tasks in accordance with their training, education, qualifications, and so on. That is my explanation. I really cannot say anything more specific to you but I'm trying to give you an answer and I don't know whether it's going to satisfy you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It certainly does provide some information, but, you see, the impression that I had was that the fact that Muslim and Croat policemen had left the SJB in Brcko was, at least in part, a result of the take-over of the police station there, so in my understanding it would be natural for the Muslim and Croat police officers to leave the station, but I would then assume that the station would be manned with Serb police officers and fully manned. But if this is not a correct description of the facts, then I would like you to tell us why not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you the answer. I'm simply presenting the factual situation. I arrived in that police station, as I said, in order to help the organisation and the structuring of the police station as well as the normalisation of the police work. What led to the fact that after the bridges on the Sava river had been destroyed, most of the Serb personnel left the police station, I'm unable to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, pertinent to the questions that you were just asking, I would direct your attention to adjudicated fact 1245 in this case. It may shed some light on it or give rise to you asking other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Back to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, where did you sleep while you were in Brcko? You said that the first night you spent in a hotel. And after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, at the upper floor of the police station, I was given a room. They put a military bed in that room and a wardrobe for my stuff. So the time that I spent in Brcko, is the time that I spent overnighting in that police station. Maybe this is not a courageous thing but it's a fact, the first night when I entered the police station, I put a heavy metal safe in front of the door, in front of my door, because I was afraid for my own security, having observed everything that was going on in the town of Brcko and in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain what is it that you saw going on in the town of Brcko outside the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, armed people, drunk people, soldiers and whatever other formations who went around shooting with open bottles. It was a terrible situation for me and that's the reason why I put that heavy metal safe in front of my door before I spent the first night in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn what kind of individuals they were? Were they paramilitary formations, military formations, or something else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly paramilitary formations. They were not under the control of the army. According to law, they should have been re-subordinated to the military and the military should have assigned them tasks. They were paramilitaries. I come back again to the Red Berets belonging to Captain Dragan and that Rade person. In Brcko they did practically whatever they wanted. Besides the paramilitary formation, units from Bijeljina used to come as well. That's when I had the opportunity for the first time to encounter the Panthers belonging to Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer. There were other structures, military or semi-military, that were completely unfamiliar to me. I spent a short period of time in Brcko and I couldn't really find out exactly who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While you stayed in Brcko did you receive any intelligence as to what was the reason for such a strong presence of so many paramilitary formations and individuals that you observed in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Brcko was one of richer municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was prosperous, it had industry, there was a harbour on the Sava river which meant that Brcko was, via the Danube, connected all the way to Vienna. So it was a prosperous municipality. All the paramilitary formations concentrated first and foremost on plunder. Let me give you a piece of information that is maybe inaccurate but that's what I heard then. 150 trucks of Marlboro cigarettes were taken away from the harbour in Brcko. There was the primary motive, plunder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was there free customs export zone in Brcko before those events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, apart from the cigarettes were there any goods that were on consignment in the customs warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I went to my following task in Bijeljina, and we are probably going to touch upon the topic later, so when my task was establishment of check-points, we would definitely come across people coming back from Brcko who in their vehicles transported alcohol, electric goods which means that customs-free zone in Brcko contained also that kind of goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to record of meeting in Brcko, the meeting that you had initiated. Was a commander of the police station appointed after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a commander was appointed. It was Mr. Petar Djokic. His deputy and two or three assistants were also appointed. I think that I proposed that Mr. Petar Djokic to Mr. Veselic to be appointed commander. I learned that he graduated from the secondary police school in Sarajevo and subsequently from the law faculty in Belgrade. He was born in Brcko, which means that he was well acquainted with the general situation in Brcko at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that on this meeting the very foundations for proper functioning of the police station in Brcko were laid?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not have old rule books at hand, for instance, the rule book on the proper way of functioning of the public security service and we didn't have the text of the law, however, we defined in brief outlines the tasks of all managerial positions in the police station. And it was to serve as some sort of aide-memoire for them and it defined the basic principles of work in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] if there are no objections, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic -- sorry, Mr. Zecevic, the meeting the witness was referring to a few minutes ago, is that the meeting in the -- is that this document, the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he confirmed that is the minutes of the first meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's on the 2nd of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have another question. Mr. Andan, the blowing up of the bridges over the Sava, we have heard information that that happened on the 30th of April. You said the beginning of April but you also said don't take me -- don't take my word on dates, so I'm wondering, would the -- could 30 April be correct as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If you can, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. As I told you, when it comes to dates they are not my strength. It's quite possible that it's the 30th. I cannot claim with any certainty that it was either on the 6th April or on the 30th of April. I simply know that it happened around about that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D546, Your Honours. 47, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, since you slept in the public security station in Brcko, after you arrived and while you stayed there did you encounter the people who were imprisoned in the public security station in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what people you are referring to. Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the people who had been detained in the station, civilians and primarily people of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not encounter anybody like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After this meeting was there -- was a practice instituted in the public security station in Brcko that certain registers should be kept?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the military granted our request and the policemen returned from the front line, the first thing that we did was to divide the area of the station in various subareas and patrol sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P153 MFI. Tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I interrupted you. Do go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we agreed to divide the station area in various sub-areas and patrol sectors. I think that on that occasion we also appointed leaders of the patrol sectors. We re-established the functioning of patrols. Normally when you say a patrol, you refer to two policemen. But because of the situation that prevailed at the time in the Brcko municipality, we reinforced the patrols so our patrols were constituted of four policemen. We also agreed that important buildings such as the municipality building and the police station should be secured by the policemen while all other points should be secured by the Territorial Defence or the army. So we tried to diminish the number of people working on security of those other facilities. After that we formed an intervention unit numbering around 30 lads. Its purpose was if there were any problems at check-points that we had established at the entrances to the town, the purpose was to be ready to help the policemen working on the check-points on short notice if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the main reason for establishment of the check-points at the entrance to the city?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The check-points had been established in order to prevent plunder and transportation of material goods from the Brcko municipality. That was the primary purpose at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still owe you one more reply. When I spoke that we re-established the registers and other log-books in the police station, we did whatever we could at the time. First and foremost we started with the daily event log. That's a document where all the events that occur within 24-hour period are registered. After that we introduced a special list where all people working in the police station were registered, as well as their tasks and assignments. Then we also introduced the criminal register, the KU book. I also proposed to introduce the daily event bulletin. It was our attempt to inform the political structures of the security situation for every 24-hour period. We did one more thing. That daily bulletin we distributed as well to the media. It means that every morning at 8.00 in the morning, the Brcko radio station was in a position to inform the citizens about all relevant events in the territory of the Brcko municipality at the time. And in the end let me mention one more thing, one more step that we undertook. We requested from the competent municipal authorities, and I refer to the political authorities here, to introduce a curfew. We informed the citizens via the Brcko radio station that a curfew would be introduced. I think that it lasted from 9.30 in the evening until 5.30 in the morning. I'm sure that this also functioned in the manner that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before moving on to comment on the documents that you introduced, tell me what the reason was for your suggestion to impose a curfew in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was again the looting of property, breaking and entering the houses of non-Serb citizens, and moving into those houses. All that would happen in the night hours in the previous period. And we wanted to protect all citizen, when I say all, whoever was in Brcko at the time. We wanted their property and their safety to be equal or to enjoy equal treatment to that of all other citizens of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know that you stayed in Brcko briefly, but did these measures yield any results as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, but the police also had some problems in that regard. The police station was attacked by paramilitaries on several occasions. Even fire-arms were used. As a result, we brought in some 40 paramilitaries in a raid and as far as I remember they had kidnapped Major Sehovac and they tried to blackmail us to release their members and they would release Major Sehovac in return. If we failed to do that, they would kill him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, we'll get to that detail yet. We have a document in front of us. It reads "Information" and it's signed by Petar Djokic, commander of the police station. This is about the situation on 8 June, as we see. At that point in time we read that the strength of the police station was 363 of which number 31 are active-duty members. Is this the situation after the military returned a number of MUP members from the front line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is this report and I only need to add that my colleagues from Brcko went to the houses and apartments of the Serbian colleagues who had left the Brcko police station and did not respond to calls. I think that there were 34 active-duty police officers and everybody else was a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, these active-duty officers, that is, the number mentioned here in this report, were those you found in Brcko, those five or six, plus the ones they went to fetch from their houses or apartments to come back to the police station. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And these members of the reserve force, that is 330 odd, were sent back from the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the reserve police force was present at the police station but probably they didn't have particular assignments. However, the majority were returned from the front line and they took up their duty at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that this -- that the MFI mark should be removed from this document unless Mr. Hannis is opposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree with that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it is, the MFI status is removed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record this is Exhibit P153.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 65 ter 181D1. Tab 9 in your binder, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, before we comment on this document you have listed the documents -- or, rather, the types of documents that were kept at the SJB of Brcko after your arrival. That list you mentioned, were you able to see it once it was established at the Brcko SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I insisted on it and that register was opened. It was kept by the deputy commander of the police station. It was a list of duty assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did that list contain the names of police officers providing security to some facilities or manning some check-points and the like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Next to the name of the officer, there was also mention of the nature of the assignment. For example, securing a facility. Mostly we used abbreviations such as OB or PS or PAT for patrol service. That is how it should have been and I think it really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, do you know that in the territory of Brcko municipality there was a collection centre or prison by the name of Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the introduction of all elements for the normalisation of the functioning of the police station, at some time toward the end of my stay, I heard of that collection centre, which was also called a camp, which was called Luka at Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know did the SJB or MUP members in general have anything to do with that Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there and according to some information from the previous period, I can say that the SJB had no authority over Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, sir, this document we see on the screens, do you know it and can you tell us who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but my signature is missing. I suppose that this report was sent to the MUP with an accompanying letter or a cover letter. This report itself is not signed but the cover letter must have been signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say it was sent to the MUP, does that mean it was sent to the Bijeljina CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the MUP of the RS sent me to Brcko, the current practice was that I was supposed to inform the administration, the relevant administration of the MUP, and that was the administration of the police, and the relevant branch of the CSB which was the Bijeljina CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this report we see, I think it's the second sentence: "Shortly after the bridges were destroyed on 30 April 1992, the operation of the station has practically stopped."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you now confirm the date of the destruction of the bridges for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, clearly this is my report, the report I drafted, and the date must be correct. And I apologise again as regards the dates, because I have already stated that I'm not good at dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence unless there's opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I perhaps request that there's an inquiry made as to whether this is the complete document because the second page ends in the middle and I don't know if there was something additional. If the witness can verify that's the total and complete report he sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You heard the question, Mr. Andan, take a look at the document, please, and then confirm that the document is complete.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document is complete and I've already explained the procedure. I've explained why my signature is missing on the second page, because probably I signed the cover letter with which this was sent to Pale and Bijeljina. However, the cover letter hasn't been shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The cover letter hasn't yet been located or has it been otherwise exhibited, what is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D548, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, tell me when and where you met Mr. Mico Davidovic for the first time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met him on an afternoon as far as I remember at the Brcko police station. He arrived in uniform in a Puh vehicle and he wanted me to give him information on the security situation in the Brcko and I made a brief presentation about what we had done and what our plans were for the coming period. As far as I remember, he then informed me that he had arrived at the Bijeljina CSB and the kind of work that we had done in Brcko should also be done at other SJBs under the CSB of Bijeljina and in Bijeljina itself, the town. And he was interested in what we had done in Brcko and what our intentions were. That was my first meeting with Mr. Mico Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was roughly, or at least which period it was when he came to see you? You have repeatedly said that you aren't good at dates.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the first half of June. May have been on the 10th or 12th or 15th, I don't know, but I think it was in the first half of June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How much time did you spend in Brcko in all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was there for two weeks, a day more or less, I don't know, but no longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to whose order did you leave Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Brcko pursuant to Cedo Kljajic's orders who at the time was undersecretary of public security and he was with the Bijeljina CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What did Cedo Kljajic order you to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first spoke on the phone as far as I remember, and he told me that my mission in Brcko was accomplished, that the basic reasons I had been sent there for were met and when I arrived at Bijeljina that we would discuss my future assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, how shall I put this, were you satisfied with what was done in Brcko over those two weeks in terms of constituting the public security station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I think I was satisfied. I haven't had an opportunity to tell you about some of the other things that we did in Brcko. If you allow me, I'm going to say that as well. In addition to this basic police activity, we constituted a crime prevention service there, we appointed the chief of the crime prevention service, and this crime prevention service started operating. As for the administrative department, we constituted that as well. We appointed a head of the administrative department. I've already said that no longer people were able to walk into the police station with a rifle and to take driver's licences, traffic licences, licence plates and so on when they were armed, so we stopped that kind of thing and citizens could go to the administrative department in a legal and legitimate way and take care of the business that they had to. Also, we established a depository. We had these certificates about things that were temporarily taken from persons. Also, for cars that were seized from various individuals, most of these vehicles had been stolen in the first place. Since the Brcko police station has this wonderful area for a kitchen, we actually made this kitchen there where all the employees of the police station were able to have a hot meal during the course of 24 hours. There were other things that we were supposed to do, but basically I was satisfied with what we did and I was satisfied with the way people treated me and also the job that we were doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 22, line 21, or rather, 20, you said that you then constituted a crime prevention service in the public security station in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We did that too. And I think that at that point in time we had six or seven operatives and a chief at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Am I understanding you correctly, namely that this crime prevention service, the crime police, had not been operating before that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had not been operating before that. I found a person there who was chief of the department of national security and the crime service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will have to take you back to tab 15. 1D547.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7 in e-court, the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Number 4, that's what the actual number on the page is, it says "Crime", that's the subheading and then the first sentence: "Tasks and work in the field of crime prevention function practically from the time when the division took place, that is the establishing of the Brcko Serb SJB."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear Mr. Zecevic's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says that a person from the national security or rather state security -- I do apologise. What I said is that in this first sentence that negation is missing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a typo? That's what it is most probably.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It's a typo, and this work was being done in most substandard conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Andan, just a few more questions in relation to Brcko, and then we are going to move on to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, this is an adjudicated fact. It is 1255.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Goran Jelisic from Brcko ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met this person but I know the name of Goran Jelisic, nicknamed Adolf. That is the how he introduced himself in Brcko and that is what the top police personnel at the public security station in Brcko said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Kosta Kole Simeunovic, a member of the police in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know this, that this certain Kosta Kole Simeunovic was, how shall I put this, in charge of the Luka camp sometime from May or June 1992 when you were in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had an objection. If he doesn't know the person then he can't know whether he was in charge of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to refresh the memory of the witness if he perhaps knows. If I give him additional information, maybe he refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps you can rephrase the question. I understand what you are trying to achieve, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that a certain Simeunovic was in May or June 1992 the person in charge of the Luka camp in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I've actually already asked you that. Thank you. Tell me, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber this is adjudicated fact 1259.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about this company, it's probably a forwarding company called Laser from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that company. It exists in the territory of Brcko to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1992 in the premises of that company Muslim and Croat civilians were detained?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I say know or aware of something, did you receive such information while you were in Brcko or subsequently when you worked in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not received such information, although in terms of our programme orientation, we were supposed to go back to Brcko with fresh forces and practically to collect all this information and intelligence and process it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of this place called Vestfalija, a restaurant that was a collection centre or prison where Muslims were held, or rather Muslim and Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the football stadium in Brcko, actually did you have any intelligence to that effect, that at the football stadium in Brcko Muslim and Croat civilians were detained during the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could I just ask you if this line of questioning is designed to challenge adjudicated fact 1259?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think, but I need to consult the rules and the guide-lines that we have adopted, but I think that there was some sort of an agreement that when you wish to challenge adjudicated facts that you let us know in advance. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he had indicated in the proofing note that he was going to address certain adjudicated facts about Brcko and Bijeljina, and I had received a copy of that. I don't know if Your Honours did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much. I was unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I sent according to the -- exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I apologise, I was not aware of the proofing note, so please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, to make this as short as possible, do you have any knowledge to the effect that Muslim and Croat civilians, during the course of 1992, were held in Brcko at the primary school in Loncari DTV Partizan and in Pelagiceva [phoen], in some shop, co-operative shop or store in Pelagiceva?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Brcko from the employees -- or, rather, did you receive from the employees of the public security station any information or intelligence about security-related incidents that they had at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Can we have a moment, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Forgive me for bringing this up again, Mr. Zecevic. I do see that in your proofing notes that you are mentioning that the witness will testify about some of these facts, including 1259. However, all information that the witness has given so far is that he doesn't know about the existence of some of the facts that are contained in that adjudicated fact, so if you have nothing more in terms of a challenge than the witness not knowing about the existence of certain buildings and so on, then I question again whether this is a useful path to proceed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if the witness can take off his earphones and I will explain. Your Honours, the witness is the inspector of the police from MUP of Republika Srpska. He comes to Brcko. He is sent from the MUP to investigate what is the situation, the security situation in Brcko. If he doesn't have the information that these detention centres exist at all in the -- in Brcko, he said he had the information about the Luka camp and he is not disputing that. He is disputing -- he is saying that the Luka camp had nothing to do with the police, but he is not disputing the existence of the Luka camp. However, he says that they had no information whatsoever that the detention centre existed on these other five or six locations in Brcko, as the adjudicated fact says. Now, if the police doesn't know that, then obviously, Your Honours, that goes for the knowledge of the MUP at its seat by all means, not only to -- not only suggesting that it is very unlikely that the adjudicated fact is a true fact if the police doesn't know about it. Surely the police should have known about the existence of such detention centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We understand the argument that you are placing yourself in a position to make and I suppose for practical purposes, the -- there is no other course open to you than the line of questions you've been asking and the questions you have been receiving from this witness, but the argument really is -- will have to come later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm sorry, I wasn't trying to make an argument. I was just trying to explain because I was invited by His Honour Judge Harhoff to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We understand. We understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour, perhaps we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, just before the break I asked you a question but your answer was not recorded because of the intervention by the Chamber. Page 27, line 18. My question went as follows: "During your stay in Brcko, did you get any information or intelligence from the employees of the public security station in Brcko related to the security-related events?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The practice before the war was as follows: When an operative comes from the fields he has to type a report. Bearing in mind that we did not have the possibility to type up reports in Brcko at the time, we agreed that at the end of each working day they should simply write out their report by pencil. Such reports were then submitted to the commander of the police station every day. He analysed them. Whatever had to be sent to the crime department, he would send to the crime department. Anything related to the public law and order and general police work, he would analyse with his associates and then issue instructions and then the following day when the police would go out, he would assign new tasks or comment on the reports written the previous days, tell the policemen what they should be alert to, and whatever else was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not want to interrupt you, my question was as follows: You said that when you arrived in Brcko, you met with the then chief, that there were five or six other people in the duty service. When you had the meeting with the chief, did you get any intelligence from him about the situation in Brcko, about what was going on in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a very extensive report but he informed me about the current security situation in Brcko, whatever was relevant for the police structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you returned to Bijeljina, to whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to the undersecretary for public security, Mr. Rajic [as interpreted], who was already in Bijeljina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that when you first arrived in Bijeljina at the end of May, Predrag Jesuric gave you the order, and we saw a document related to that, to go to Brcko. Do you remember whether Mr. Jesuric was still in Bijeljina when you returned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When describing your first arrival you said that you saw a certain Dragan Devedlaka. When you returned from Brcko was Mr. Devedlaka still in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not in Bijeljina. As far as I know in May when I saw him and when he told me that I should flee from Brcko, he left, he arrived to -- he arrived in Serbia, and he never returned to the territory of Republika Srpska or Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He warned you to flee from Brcko --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, just an intervention on the transcript if I could. I think at page 30, line 23, the last name is incorrectly recorded, if we could clarify that before we move too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The undersecretary for public security to whom you reported, we have his name recorded as Rajic. What was exactly the name as the undersecretary for public security that was already in Bijeljina at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's misinterpreted. The name is Kljajic, not Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 31, I asked you about Dragan Devedlaka, and you said, as far as I know in May when I saw him, and when he told me that I should flee from Brcko, he left to Serbia and never returned to the territory of Republika Srpska or Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did Dragan Devedlaka told you to flee from Brcko or from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to make a mistake but I think that I said also the first time to flee from Bijeljina. Maybe it's wrong interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It wasn't wrong interpretation, you misspoke.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What assignment were you given upon your return in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we waited for Mr. Mico Davidovic. He was already in Bijeljina. We had a meeting. At that meeting we defined our further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your further activities, could you explain briefly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station or the security centre in Bijeljina faced many problems. The situation had to be stabilised within the police station, and our other goal, which is defined in the Law on the Interior is the protection of citizens and property, prevention of plunder, expulsion of persons, and other criminal offences that we are probably going to discuss later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to the information you received at the meeting what is your opinion -- what was the situation that you faced in Bijeljina at the time, or maybe perhaps you should first tell us exactly what time-period you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I spent two weeks at most in Brcko, so it could have been the end of the first half of June 1992. The situation in Bijeljina was very difficult. There were significant political problems. There were two paramilitary formations that had not been re-subordinated to the military. They attempted to dominate the government structures of Bijeljina. I refer here to the Panthers led by Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, and the Serb Volunteer Guard led by Vojvoda Mirko Blagojevic. This internal conflict had consequences on the security situation in Bijeljina. They attempted to impose their personnel in the police station and in the security centre in Bijeljina. They wanted to control the work of the security centre in Bijeljina by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So having learned all this, what did you do or attempt to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether in the meantime a dispatch had arrived from the Ministry of the Interior in Pale in which it was ordered explicitly that all persons with criminal files who were currently in the Ministry of the Interior and the policemen for whom it can be proved that they took part in criminal activities had to be eliminated from the Ministry of the Interior. So I'm not quite sure whether it was before or after dispatch, but we did that in accordance with the law. We carried out the so-called triage of the policemen and removed around 40 policemen from the force. Later it led to anger and the pressure exerted on me and other employees of the police station. I can elucidate on that later if you want me to. So this was the first step that we took in the police station in Bijeljina. We dealt with the internal order and organisation again. We established high criteria for entrance into the police station that pertained to various military and paramilitary formations carrying long barrels. That is to say, we did not allow people to enter the police station with long barrels. We did the same thing that we did in Brcko. They had to deposit their weapons upon entering the police station. They would receive a certificate and then they would get it back upon leaving. After that we analysed the division of the area belonging to the public security station in Bijeljina. We worked out an appropriate division into sub-areas and patrol sectors. They were all preliminary tasks that had to be done before operative actions that would follow. We did not have to introduce new documents in Bijeljina and by that I mean the daily event log, the register, the KU register, all this existed in the police station in Bijeljina, however, it wasn't filled in in an appropriate way until we arrived and issued strict orders in relation to that. So in this area as well we issued strict orders that everything that happened within a 24-hour period should be recorded. We also started issuing a daily event bulletin. Every morning at 8.00 in the morning, we would distribute it to the media. There was, if I remember correctly, a radio station called Radio Semberija and Majevica. We would deliver our bulletin to them every morning so that the citizens in Bijeljina municipality could be apprised of all the events that had occurred within the previous 24 hours in the territory or the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, did the public security station Bijeljina and the Security Services Centre Bijeljina share the same building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they shared the building. The police station was on the ground floor, the premises of the security centre were on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we go into details with regard to the situation in Bijeljina, I would like to take a look at P338, tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, this is a report on inspection conducted and situation found at SJB Brcko, SJB Zvornik, and partially the situation at SJB Bijeljina. The date is the 17th of June, 1992, and on the last page we see your name and your signature. As well as the name and signature of Danilo Vukovic. Mr. Andan, is this your report that was submitted to the Ministry of the Interior on the 17th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a joint report made by you and Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, if you allow me -- oh, it was corrected. First it was Vukotic in the transcript and now it's Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, can we take a look at 65 ter 13D1, tab 27. Let us wait for the English translation of the document. This is a document originating from the Ministry of the Interior dated the 24 of June 1992, sent to the Bijeljina public security station. If you take a look at the signature, tell us whether you can recognise it, and do you know what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a request sent to the police station in Bijeljina. It relates to some police inspector, I don't know whether somebody came from Sarajevo or whether it was some sort of inspection, but the crux of the matter is that that person needed a vehicle. I'm not sure about the signature, but I think that it could be the signature of Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this document relate to you or to Danilo or to somebody else, some other inspector? When I say Danilo, I refer to Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this document had nothing to do with us because in the existing police station we already had had the cars that we could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 145D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Andan, you explained that after the meeting in Bijeljina, you undertook certain measures, and what were the main directions of those measures. Did you undertake any other measures in the field, and if so, which other measures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must inform you that we also forwarded the information to the media that a curfew was being imposed in Bijeljina from 9.30 p.m. through 5.30 a.m., and that it was published in the media and the objective was the same, to prevent looting, illegal entering of other people's homes, and many other criminal offences that were committed at night in the Bijeljina municipality too. We set up check-points at points of entry and exit, manned by police, to prevent the transportation of stolen goods from other municipalities or out of that municipality. Brcko was the most prosperous municipality and most of the goods originated from there. And to reach Bijeljina they had to cross either Pavlovica Most or the Raca border crossing to enter Serbia. We set up such check-points at practically all points of entry into Bijeljina or points of exit. The staff manning those check-points had instructions to seize all stolen goods and detain persons carrying them. Certificates for seized goods were issued and the goods themselves were placed in the gymnasium of the police station. We found a large plateau near Radio Yugoslavia where we placed the stolen vehicles, whereas the small items such as gold and jewellery were deposited in the strongbox at the Bijeljina police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have a document dated 28 June 1992 on our screens. It's a report of the public security service for 26 and 27 June 1992. On page 3 of this document we read your name. Can you tell us more about this document, what it's about. It's under tab 31.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the reports that should be there in accordance with the agreement and pursuant to the legislation in force, we seized stolen items and goods from persons coming from other municipalities to Bijeljina. This is just an example of things that were seized on that day. The persons mentioned here were taken to the police station and processed whereas the goods were deposited and appropriate documents were drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since we see your name typed here but there is no signature, was it a document that was drafted pursuant to your instructions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is probably the same principle. There must have been a cover letter because I see here that we not only sent this to the relevant department but we also copied the president of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina, the garrison commander of Bijeljina and other structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly why I would like you to comment on the last paragraph of this document before the distribution list, if you can.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are stating here that we will continue the processing of these suspects and submit criminal reports to the prosecutor's office. We are hereby making it clear that honest people can feel safe in the Bijeljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you are saying honest people, does that include non-Serbs too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was our duty under the law. We couldn't discriminate on racial or any other grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document unless there's opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D549, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the following document, 65 ter 146D1. That's tab 38 in your binder. Can you tell us what this is about and what kind of activity preceded this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had intelligence that in the refrigeration plant, the construction of which began before the war, I forget the exact name of that location, that this refrigeration plant was used by Mauzer and his Panthers as a storage facility for stolen goods. We checked that information and then we made a plan. We raided the place and we expected armed resistance on the part of the Panthers who were guarding that warehouse. Fortunately, the raid was well organised, or perhaps they were too confused, but they didn't have a chance to use their weapons, so we overpowered them and locked them up in a room. I think that we also informed the prosecutor that we were about to search the place in accordance with the regulations. These documents show what we found in that warehouse that was kept by Mauzer. I needn't list the items, you can see the list yourself, but both Mr. Davidovic and I were flabbergasted by something. Since this refrigeration plant was under construction and the cooling chambers were already finished but there was no electricity, there was a large aluminium door. I opened one of these doors without any particular intention and found three men inside. They seemed exhausted and haggard and I asked them who they were but they were probably too afraid to say anything. We took them out, we gave them some water and one of them said that his name was Imsirovic and that the others were his brothers, that a few days ago, a group of soldiers under the command of Mauzer had taken them prisoner in the house in Bijeljina where they lived and taken them to this place. They recognised Mico Davidovic who lived in -- nearby and he confirmed their identity. We couldn't provide full protection for them. We couldn't have police standing guard in front of their house, but we took them home in a patrol car. We suggested to them that they should leave and go to live with some relatives because probably Mauzer would be back and then the result would be much worse for them. After many years while I was subject to OHR sanctions, one of the three Imsirovic brothers called me on the phone from Austria and he said that he was willing to make a statement to any prosecutor's office. He also said that his two brothers were also alive and that on that night they had crossed the Sava to Serbia and moved on to Austria and Germany. One of the three brothers was in Germany, the other in Austria, and the third one at Zivinice. He also called me on the phone and said that he was willing to help me if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These Imsirovic brothers, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims, and still are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document reads, it's a list of items that were stolen and that were stored at the new slaughter-house in Obarska, is that the place you meant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do with these goods that you seized on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mauzer's unit should have been re-subordinated to the VRS according to the command structure, and we gave these items to the army. I see that it was confirmed here that the army -- that there was this hand-over to the army, and what they did with that later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document unless there is objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D550, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, could I, just out of curiosity, ask you what happened to the members of Mauzer's Panthers? Did you arrest them and do you know if they were prosecuted for having stolen all these things and detained illegally, I suppose, three Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry that I laughed when you asked this question but there is a he a good reason for that. We arrested Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer, and we placed him in remand custody. We took away his side-arm which was a Heckler with a silencer. And then Mauzer's entire unit attacked the police station with tanks and all weapons that they had at their disposal. Then we set up circular Defence in a military fashion and defended ourselves to prevent Mauzer from entering the police station. That went on for a couple of hours until the municipal authorities arrived, spoke to Mr. Kljajic, Mr. Davidovic, and me, and found a Solomonic solution to release Mauzer from detention and then the forces that had surrounded the police station would withdraw. That's what we did and I believe that we thus avoided an armed conflict. Savic was released from detention but we didn't return his Heckler. It remained at the police station. That's how we solved the problem. Don't lay me down on this, but I think that a report was made to the prosecutor's office for the criminal offences committed by Mauzer, but I don't know what happened later, you can believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, do you know of the murder of one Salko Kukic in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at 65 ter 350D1. That's tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an on-site investigation report dated 2 June 6 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina. It was drafted by the investigative magistrate, or rather, the persons present for the investigative magistrate, the representative of a Bijeljina prosecutor's office and two representatives of the Bijeljina SJB. I know that you weren't in Bijeljina at the time but were you able to see this document later as part of a file?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this document. This did not happen while I was in Bijeljina, I was in Brcko at the time, but on the basis of this document and on the basis of intelligence we took further operative measures aimed at arresting the perpetrators of this heinous crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D551, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D -- actually, 65 ter 352D1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 21. Tell me, sir, the late Salko Kukic was an ethnic Muslim, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the crime service once they found out that Slavko -- that Salko Kukic had been murdered provided information to the then prosecutor and on site they compiled photo documentation that is part of the file and it shows the scene of the crime, that is to say the murder of Mr. Kukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is tab 11. 65 ter 351D1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 11. Sir, this is an official record concerning an interview with Aziza Kukic in relation to the murder of her son, Salko Kukic. Are you familiar with this official record and this lady, Mrs. Kukic? Was she an eye-witness of the crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the official record but I have to say that this was usual practice for operatives. They probably compiled this record although it hasn't been signed. It has to do with the collection of all relevant data and of course Ms. Aziza was also interviewed and she speaks about how the murder took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This Official Note, is it a document that was compiled by the members of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's for sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's tab 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, no objection, Your Honour, although I don't see the relevance. I don't think there's any issue here that this murder was investigated. We have several other documents in evidence already that that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you are not challenging that the police was doing their proper job in this case, I'm not going to tender any more evidence on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we are challenging that there was what appears to be a proper investigation into the murder of Salko Kukic by the local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at document 65 ter 359D1. That is tab 102 in your binder. Sir, this is a decision dated the 3rd of August, 1992. It is a ruling on detention and is signed by Dragan Andan, chief of public security station. There is a signature and a stamp. Is this a document of yours and what is it about actually, what does this decision on detention actually refer to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We continued working on the case of Salko Kukic's murder and through our operative activity we came to the conclusion that four perpetrators had committed this heinous crime. We brought these persons into the police station in Bijeljina. We took them into custody. They were detained and you see that these are decisions on their detention. That is to say, for these four persons. There are two here, though, but there should be two more. Then we also filed a criminal report where we dealt with all four persons, all the crimes committed, all the charges involved and I think that the date was the 3rd of August, 1992. It was sent on to the prosecutor's office. So we solved the case of this murder. We found the perpetrators, we filed a criminal report, we handed them over to the prosecutor's office and this is where our authority ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, as for these four individuals, Istok Pojatar is the one referred to in this particular document, he is one of the suspects in the murder case of the late Salko Kukic. To the best of your knowledge what is Mr. Istok Pojatar's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know all four of them are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence. Unfortunately, the remaining three documents that are decisions on detention or custody for those three persons are separate exhibits. Now, I don't know what Mr. Hannis's view is.
