If he would accept that in relation to all of these suspects who were detained by the Ministry of the Interior, if he agrees, I wouldn't tender the other documents. These are documents in tabs 100, 101, and 103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But even in respect of this, Mr. Zecevic, I'm somewhat at a loss as to the utility of it as an exhibit. It is an example of the witness doing his job in the ordinary course of what one would expect. What -- for what purpose do we need the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And Mr. Hannis in his -- in respect of the previous document has indicated that they take no issue with what ordinarily happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was about to say, Your Honour, I don't have an objection to one of these as an example because this doesn't relate so much to the fact that an investigation occurred but it has to do with the process of the police being able to make an initial decision about detention which I think is something that we are interested in having evidence about. So I don't object to this one as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D552, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now, I am not sure what is the position of Mr. Hannis concerning the documents 65 ter 356D1, 357D1 and 358D1 which are tabs 101, 100 and 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any objection to them either. I just don't know that they are necessary because they are simply the rulings on detention as to the other two named individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Other three named individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't object to them coming in, I just don't think they are necessary to make the point I want to make from a document like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said that a criminal report had been filed. 1D105, tab 104. Could you please just confirm that that is the document concerned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who signed this document on your behalf? Can you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Danilo Vukovic signed this for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please give us your comment on document 65 ter 355D1. That is tab 37. This is a report on solving the murder for gain of Salko Kukic in Bijeljina in early June 1992. It is signed by Danilo Vukovic. Are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who is this submitted to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going back to what practice is and what is envisaged in the rules and organisation of the Ministry of the Interior. If the centre is the protagonist of the activity related to certain information, then it it is our duty to inform the appropriate administrations within the Ministry of the Interior by way of providing such information. It happened quite often that we sent this kind of information to the minister of the interior. So the minister does not have any particular authority in this respect. Of course he has authority, but as for the practical part, he can send this on to the administrations and say, Administrations, you do your job now, or he can just say thank you to whoever sent the information. So the primary goal was to provide information to the appropriate administrations that were supposed to deal with the particular case that was ultimately solved in the way this one was solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections I would like to move that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D553, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, we saw just now this documentation that is related to this crime committed against a member of the Muslim people, the late Salko Kukic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Salko Kukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Salko Kukic, yes. You established during the investigation that the perpetrators were four individuals of Serb ethnicity. We saw that procedure was carried out as you had explained to us. Tell us, the way in which the public security station of Bijeljina acted, is that something that was applied in all other cases as well when grave crimes were committed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We treated all cases in the same way. However, due to imminent threat of war, we sometimes intervened ad hoc. Actually, I'm going to give you an example. A person of Muslim ethnicity, a vet, came to the police station to report that the members of Mauzer's unit in the town of Bijeljina stopped him right in town and took away his car, which was a Golf. We intervened by sending an intervention team into town to find the car on the basis of its licence plates. They found the car, they brought it to the police station, then they called the gentleman. I really don't know his name but he spent the entire war in Bijeljina, and he came to pick up his car. So this was this kind of ad hoc protection, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My question was about grave crimes, murder, against life and limb and so on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, I have already given you an answer that we treated them all the same way. All crimes were treated in a highly professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did the ethnicity of the victim or the perpetrator have any influence on you or any consequences?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood the question properly, you are asking me whether we treated all the ethnicities in the same manner. Of course, we treated all the ethnicities in Bijeljina in the same manner throughout the period that Mr. Davidovic and I spent in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Bijeljina, while you were the chief of the public security station, were there any cases in which the police did not investigate an offence and undertake appropriate measure because the injured party was a non-Serb or the assumed perpetrator was a Serb? Were there any cases like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm testifying under oath here and I claim under full responsibility that in that period there was not a single case that you describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When we discussed the action in the slaughter-house, you told us that Mr. Mico Davidovic was with you. This unit of Mico Davidovic, how many men were in the unit and where did they hail from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 25 to 30 men in the unit, that is a platoon strength. They came from the federal SUP in Belgrade. It was called Yugoslavia then and not Serbia and Montenegro. They came pursuant to a request by government or the minister of the interior in order to assist in the security centre in Bijeljina in order to prevent all forms of crime, in order to prevent -- to guarantee the right to property and life of all the citizens and all other things stipulated by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, do you remember that you received an order from the Ministry of the Interior on the decrease of the number of the reserve policemen while you were the chief of the public security station in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that, in accordance with the dispatch that had arrived from the Ministry of the Interior, we acted upon it and agreed that we should first of all remove all persons with a criminal file. However, this was a very difficult process in the police station in Bijeljina. And if you would allow me, I'd like to explain exactly how we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we knew there were more than 1.000 members of the reserve police force. We analysed the membership and concluded that various mama's and papa's boys sought shelter there, as well as other persons whose intention was not to be sent to the front line. So we reached an internal agreement. I think Mr. Kljajic, Mr. Davidovic, and I agreed that on a certain day, I don't remember the date anymore, we would call up the complete reserve police force. We agreed to draft a false document which would then be read out before the reserve police. That is, when they gather, a policeman would arrive and read out a dispatch which would contain, inter alia, the following: That the front line had had been breached in the area of Teocak and that additional forces from Bijeljina were needed to reinforce that part of the line urgently in order to stabilise the whole front line. So I read out this document. I told them that nobody had an obligation to respond, but those who wanted to join me and march towards Teocak should stand on my right side and all of them on the left side. Approximately two-thirds of them stood on the left side. And then I immediately ordered that all the weapons and equipment should be taken away from all those who stood on the left. I told them that this was a false alert. Then I ordered the active force of the police to escort them through the town all the way to the barracks and hand them over to the VRS. The remainder of the reserve police force we checked against the crime files. There were some people who had crime files and we simply told them to go away and that is how we managed to form the core of the new police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps as I'm moving to another field, maybe it's a proper time to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, during July 1992, did you return to Brcko at any point in time or did you carry out any action in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't only me. The Mico Davidovic's unit, reinforced with some forces that had arrived in the meantime in agreement with Cedo Kljajic and the minister, carried out an action. The reason for that was the fact that the integrity of the police station had again been breached and we simply had to intervene in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 154D1, tab 57. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is your memo, or at least your name is typed. The date is the 20th of July, 1992. It was sent to the Ministry of the Interior. Can you tell us something about the two last paragraphs. They are related to the action in Brcko and I'd like you to explain briefly what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left Brcko, a number of attacks were carried out against the police station in Brcko. Members of the Red Berets were dissatisfied with the situation and with the lawful work of the police station in Brcko. They were Captain Dragan's Red Berets and they carried out a number of attacks in order to take over the police station Brcko so that they could again have free access to registration plates, identification cards, passports, and other similar stuff. So this is the information that we received. We agreed that we should carry out an action in Brcko in order to stop their activities once and for all. Our goal was to arrest them, disarm them, and to transport them in a bus to the border crossing, the border with Serbia, and to hand them over to the competent organs of Serbia. During that action in Brcko more than 30 persons were arrested. The remaining part of this paramilitary formation undertook an unlawful arrest or kidnapping of the representatives of the Brcko authorities, including the Chief of Staff of a brigade belonging to the VRS. His name was Mr. Sehovac. Negotiations ensued. They managed to gain access to our communications system and requested the release of all their arrested members. In exchange they offered the persons that they detained or arrested. In the beginning we did not release any of the members of the paramilitary formation but we managed to get the release of the representatives of the Brcko authorities; the only person who remained in their hands was Major Sehovac. Then through our communications channels, they got in contact with me and requested that Major Sehovac be released in exchange for their people. I was told that if we did not do that, that they would kill Major Sehovac. I replied in a rather laconic way. I told them go ahead, do it. Go ahead and kill him because if we Serbs have something in abundance, it's officers. Indeed we have a surplus of them. A wait ensued for more than two hours and after two hours they agreed to release Major Sehovac. A part of the unit managed to escape towards Ugljevik. The remainder surrendered. We disarmed them, as I told you, and at that point in time their only request was to be permitted to take their side-arms with them to Serbia. I'm referring here to their pistols. However, we did not allow that. We drew up a list of them and they were escorted by the police to the border crossing of Raca where they were handed over to the competent authorities belonging to the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. Among other things, we searched their premises where we discovered a lot of loot. It was their warehouse for various technical equipment and duty-free goods that they had plundered before. All this we kept in the police station in Brcko. So, that was the end of the police action in Brcko which resulted in the continuation of normal functioning and work of the police station in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D554, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the beginning of this answer, page 53, you said: "Yes, but it wasn't only me. It was Mico Davidovic's unit reinforced with the forces that had arrived in the meantime pursuant to an agreement between Cedo Kljajic and minister and they carried out this action. The reason for that was the integrity of the police station in Brcko" and so on and so forth. When you said that those forces arrived in accordance with an agreement between Cedo Kljajic and the minister, what forces were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that it all happened very quickly, all those events in the area of Semberija and Majevica. You know, the security situation in one municipality would be improved and then it would immediately deteriorate in some other municipality, so we simply could not intervene with only 30 people in the whole area of Semberija and Majevica. This is the problem that we presented to Mr. Kljajic. We asked him that he should take, if possible, a part of the special unit from Pale or some other special unit and bring it to Bijeljina in order for them to help us in carrying out our tasks. Mr. Kljajic agreed and members of such a unit arrived in Bijeljina, I don't know on which day, and they were led by Mr. Malovic, his first name may be Dusko. So in accordance with this agreement, he was re-subordinated to the command of myself and Mr. Davidovic. He took part in several actions that we carried out in the area of Semberija and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, if you remember how many members were in this unit led by Dusko Malovic, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My estimate is not more than 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where was this unit billeted upon their arrival in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no available accommodation. The military was not in a position to give them part of the barracks. We decided to accommodate the unit on the premises of the security centre in Bijeljina in our attic. We brought some cots in the attic and since there was a kitchen that functioned practically around the clock on the premises of the security centre, and since there were showers available in the gym, we simply agreed that the unit should be accommodated on the premises of the security centre in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said on page 56, line 2 and 3 that they took part in a number of actions in the territory of Semberija and Majevica. Tell us which actions were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, that was the action carried out in Brcko, the disarming of the paramilitary formations belonging to Captain Dragan. After that there was a kidnap case in Brcko. It was again some Red Berets, and I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly which Red Berets. Mirko Blagojevic, member of the Serbian Radical Party was kidnapped. Those lads wearing red berets came in two Land Rovers. They took Mirko Blagojevic in one of the Land Rovers with the intention to transport him out of the area. Later on we heard that Mirko was supposed to be executed. However, at the time we did not know that. We intervened by intercepting the vehicles, surrounding them and the members of the Red Berets pointed their long barrels at us and there was a stand-off. We were very, very close to an armed conflict. I proposed to Mr. Davidovic that I should drop my side-arm, raise my arms in the air, and approach the members of the Red Berets in order to negotiate with them. And that's what I did. They accepted me as such. I requested them to release Blagojevic. Then he -- then they told me, well, if we release Blagojevic, you are going to kill us all here. The discussion went on for a number of hours. I promised them that they would be unharmed. We arrived in the police station in Bijeljina. We released Mr. Blagojevic, and then after that we gave the police escort, I think it was Mr. Malovic's unit, we gave the police escort to the Red Berets and handed them over at the border crossing. So was that the second action. And the third action in which they directly took part was the elimination of the paramilitary formation of Yellow Wasps in Zvornik. They weren't literally liquidated, they were just arrested and proceedings were instituted against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have just said while you were speaking about Mauzer and the situation when his unit was going to attack the Bijeljina SJB with tanks. Do you remember whether Malovic's unit was in Bijeljina at the time and whether it took part in the defence of the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer, that is, his unit attacked the police station three times. Mr. Malovic and his unit took part in the defence of the police station twice, or the defence of the CSB. There was a memorable instance, the second or third attack, I think, doesn't matter really. We put up a circular defence of the building, military style, and since the building has a flat roof, some members of his unit went up there and at one moment we heard a strong explosion. Everybody lay down, ducked. They thought that a grenade fired from a tank had hit the building. Then a few moments later, I went out of the police station and that things were the same as before. One of Malovic's men had accidently activated a hand-held rocket-launcher and it had pierced a reinforced concrete wall which was 50 to 60 centimetres thick. And later we discussed how that weapon was uncarefully used at that moment. It could have been -- it could have prompted an attack against a police station by Mauzer and his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that when Malovic's unit came to Brcko and reported to Undersecretary Cedo Kljajic that it was agreed then that they should be re-subordinated to Mico Davidovic and you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, can I confirm it was to Brcko or to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us where that unit came?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to Bijeljina. I have said that already. And they were re-subordinated to our unit. First they took part in the operation in Brcko and returned to Bijeljina with us. And in Bijeljina we continued our activities and they were also billeted in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since that unit took part in a number of operations and they were -- they were there all the time, they were billeted at the Bijeljina CSB, what was their professional attitude in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discipline in that unit was surprising, and that discipline was imposed by Mr. Malovic. I remember an incident when one of his subordinates returned from town intoxicated and Malovic first gave him a good dressing down and then he slapped him on the face which was surprising to all of us. I told him that this was the last time he aced that way and if he should do that again he would be removed from the unit and returned to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While you were there and that unit was re-subordinated to Mico Davidovic's unit, were there any complaints about their conduct as MUP members?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that accurately states the evidence. I believe the witness has testified it was re-subordinated to Mico Davidovic and the witness. If I'm wrong about that, I stand corrected, but now he is only talking about Mico Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You did say to Mico Davidovic's unit and me, but do answer my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I represented the MUP of the RS, Mico Davidovic was helping out and the two of us co-ordinated all activities. That unit was re-subordinated to the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My question was did you have any complaints about their conduct as MUP members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While carrying out any operations at Majevica and Semberija, I had no complaints. They went about their job very professionally. Since we patrolled the territory during the curfew, I had the opportunity to patrol with some members of that unit and even then I had no objections to their work. Whether anything happened later, I don't know, but I'm sure that it would have been reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that this unit was sometimes referred to as Mico Stanisic's unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A number of MUP members and commanding officers called it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they called it Mico Stanisic's unit, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The composition of the unit, or rather, the unit was composed of people from the same municipality as that from which Mr. Stanisic hailed, and that's Sokolac. Nobody said that he was from Pale or Bijeljina. And that's why they called it Mico Stanisic's unit because they were all from the Sokolac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, sir, you have just spoken about the situation in the Majevica and Semberija area. You said that when the situation improved in one municipality it deteriorated in another. When I say situation, I mean security. Did you and the members of that unit which was in Bijeljina go to other municipalities in the Semberija-Majevica area too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, because we were receiving information from other municipalities as well. And I think that the basic reason for any instance of deteriorated security situation in Semberija and Majevica and from experience I can add, in many other parts of the RS were paramilitaries. They were disrupting the usual practice. Certainly in accordance with the circumstances at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Talking about these other municipalities, did you go to Lopare and Ugljevik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that we were experienced police officers and depending on the nature of the situation, we tried to get information about other municipalities in different ways. And when we did get information, we tried to check it through our members by sending them there to stay for a couple of days, gather intelligence, and then we would consider the situation at that mini-collegium. We went to Lopare, Ugljevik, Zvornik, and eventually we were supposed to go to Bosanski Samac where there were problems with one Lugar and one Crni, but for some reasons we never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say for some reason, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be specific. We didn't go because in the latter half of August 1992 Mico Davidovic's unit was withdrawn from Semberija and Majevica and I was prohibited to continue working for the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me, what was the situation in the Lopare and Ugljevik municipalities? You have already spoken about Samac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like a carbon copy. That is the situation was always the same with paramilitaries. As far as I remember in Ugljevik there were problems with some paramilitary unit I don't quite remember, and in Ugljevik there were some problems with the manning of the reserve forces of both the police and the military. There were many problems in both these municipalities and the cause of these problems were always paramilitaries that were refusing to resubordinate to the military. And of course it was impossible for them to be re-subordinated to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that at one point in early July, your unit arrested some members of the VRS? Actually, you took them in and detained them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Brought them in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember that case without looking at documents. An active duty major of the VRS was stopped at a check-point, I think it was Jovan Micic, I'm not sure about his first name but the last name is correct. On his truck and it was a large military truck, a 150 type as we called them, a lot of stolen goods were found, and they were brought to the Bijeljina police station. The goods were seized, a certificate was issued, and the goods were stored at the Bijeljina police station. That night we could not communicate with the military police and that is why Mr. Micic was detained at the police station in the Detention Unit. After that problems ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, let me show you a document. P79/41 [as interpreted]. Or rather, that's -- 41 is the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You began talking about problems so I just wanted to give an illustration. You can continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P579. This is not the document I need. 65 ter 169 of the Prosecution. This is it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a lawful police action, we brought in the major and kept him in custody until the morning when we handed him over to the military police. Some of the military structures did not like what we did and they protested primarily because the major was detained and this is what this dispatch says. Actually, the minister at the time, Mr. Stanisic, asked for some additional information with regard to the detention of Mr. Micic and this is yet further proof of the fact that we did act lawfully at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, it is P580 and P581. That is what the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could I please have your comment with regard to 65 ter 149D1. That is tab 48. This is information from the 7th of July. This information is from the 7th of July, 1992, and it says: "Report on the taking into custody and detention of Major Jovan Micic and a group of soldiers."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and attached to this report is the list of goods that we had taken on that occasion, or rather, seized. This report is a result of our activity and this is the report that was sent to the Ministry of the Interior by way of information, so that we could, inter alia, justify everything we did in terms of bringing into custody Mr. Micic. Again I'm saying that the accompanying document is missing, but in terms of hierarchy, we were duty-bound to provide information to the proper line of work within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D555, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 147. Could you please be shown 65 ter 147D1, tab 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the previous answer you mentioned a list as part of that report. This is some list of items found in a TAM E-1948 vehicle. Can you tell us what this list is all about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of that report, the one that we've already admitted, it says attachment 12. If we have already seen that. I think that that attachment is a list of the things that were found that night with Major Micic and the soldiers that we brought into custody, who was remanded in custody until the morning, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the list that we see in front of us, the list of things that were seized?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the assortment of goods that they took along with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just have a question about the relevance but I don't oppose to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't oppose it on authenticity grounds. I'm not sure how relevant it is. It's a list of a lot of household goods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going to say that I appreciate that from the witness's answer that this is an annex to the document as previously admitted, but by -- but what does it add?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is a list of the goods that were taken from this Micic, Officer Micic's unit within the army truck, and by looking at the list of the goods, it's obvious that this confirms that there was a looting going on a big scale going on in this case, and since this is the annex of the previous document, I think it's relevant that we see what the goods were found in the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. Admitted and marked. I suppose there is some utility to the breadth of items which are contained in this list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D556, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, I have a few questions in relation to adjudicated facts in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, it is 1434 actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, were you aware of the existence of a camp in Batkovici near Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did you hear of the existence of this camp for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stayed in Brcko, I asked the then chief of national security, Mr. Gavrilovic, about a friends of mine from Sarajevo, a certain Anto Vidovic who was a football player in Jedinstvo from Brcko. When I first asked him he just shrugged his shoulders. I persisted in asking what had happened to Anto, quite simply he had told me he had been taken to the camp in Batkovic, I asked him where that camp was and he said the camp is in the territory of the municipality of Bijeljina. That is the first time that I heard of the Batkovic camp. Since we had co-operation with the command of the Eastern Bosnian corps whose commander was Colonel Ilic, during an evening briefing, that is to say, from time to time we went to see them and to exchange information, I availed myself of that opportunity. Since the Batkovic camp was under the command of the military, I availed myself of that opportunity and asked Mr. Ilic to do me a favour by releasing Mr. Anto Vidovic from that camp, of course, unless he had committed a crime like murder or something else. A few days later, in the evening, I received a call from the police station and I was told that a certain individual was waiting for me at the police station all day, and when I got there, I found Mr. Anto Vidovic at the police station. Of course, this was a scene that one cannot ever forget. I went -- I went home with him, we had dinner, the next day I took him to Brcko. We went to the police station in Brcko. I said that this was a friend of mine. Since he was a car electrician by vocation, I told him -- I said that they could use him either in the army or in the police for repairing trucks, and I said that I would hold them responsible for Anto Vidovic. The war was over and Anto Vidovic survived and the first thing he did when the war was over was to go to Sarajevo to see my mother to thank her for what I had done. So this is what I had to say in relation to your question about the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, do you know that in Bijeljina, that to say in the territory of the municipality of Bijeljina, in addition to the camp in Batkovic, there were six other collection centres in the territory of the municipality including the building of the SUP in Bijeljina where Croat and Muslim civilians were detained --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just for the record, the adjudicated fact my English says six detention centres shall rather than collection centres. I don't know if it's a significant difference, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think I said six detention centres.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in Bijeljina, that is to say from mid-June until the second half of August, I claim with full responsibility that at the police station and on the premises of the Bijeljina CSB there was not a single individual, at least we did not find anyone there who had been detained on any grounds whatsoever. As for other collection centres or camps as the Prosecutor said, I did not learn of any except for the one, the camp in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For a while you were acting chief of the public security station in Bijeljina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was acting chief of the public security station and the CSB, depending on what was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The territory that was covered by the public security station of Bijeljina is the territory of the municipality of Bijeljina; right? Does it cover the territory of the municipality of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station does cover the territory of the municipality of Bijeljina and the security centre covers several municipalities in the area of Semberija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that in the territory of the municipality there were six collection centres, or rather, detention centres for detaining Croat and Muslim civilians without you knowing about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going back to the period in which we operated in the area and I claim with full responsibility that at the time these collection centres or camps that you refer to did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, the concept on the basis of which you worked in Bijeljina together with Mico Davidovic's unit and these reinforcements that were there, was it actually your concept to deal with the paramilitaries in the territory of the CSB Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was our concept. Practically we first materialised this concept in the area of Brcko, and then we planned to continue with this concept in Ugljevik and Lopare. There was a dilemma there as to who Zvornik belonged to, whether it belonged to the CSB of Bijeljina or the CSB of the Sarajevo Romanija region, I don't know what their name was. At the time in Bijeljina we believed that Zvornik was ours, whereas the people from Sarajevo thought it was theirs. One dispatch was sent by the minister of the interior in which it was stated that this centre belonged to the Sarajevo Romanija region. However, in spite of that, we did plan and carry out a major operation of neutralising the paramilitary unit called Yellow Wasps in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if you remember, when was this operation in Zvornik against the Yellow Wasps carried out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I'm going to apologise because of the dates. Dates are not all that relevant to me and I don't remember them, but I remember details that are probably relevant for this Court as well. We received a series of information about the behaviour, behaviour under quotation marks, of that paramilitary unit and we weren't sure whether all this information that we had obtained was all that reliable. At one of these collegium meetings in the morning, I was given a task to change into civilian clothing, to take a few operatives with me, and to infiltrate myself, as we say in professional terms, into Zvornik and try to obtain the information that we needed. As I arrived in Zvornik, I organised a meeting with the chief of national security, Goran Zugic, and we held this meeting in Mali Zvornik. Because our information said that the members of the Yellow Wasps paramilitary unit were following all important persons who were holders of important offices in Zvornik. In the territory of Zvornik, I stayed for about three or four days and I established exactly all the locations where Zuco, Pivarski, and another group were stationed, but because the Zuce were so numerous and because they had committed such terrible crimes, we went after the Yellow Wasps first. That's when I presented my report. What followed was a planned activity that we embarked upon. Of course before any operation one has to plan. We made a comprehensive plan that we verified at one of these morning meetings of ours, not to call them a collegium. I don't know the exact date, but I know that it was in the early morning hours that we set out to implement that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P317, item 22, tab 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, this document is dated the 20th of July, 1992. Your name and position, chief of Bijeljina CSB is typed in the signature block, it says that it was delivered to the minister and the undersecretary for public security. The subject is "information on security situation in the region of Serbia municipality Zvornik." Is this your document and is this the information that you drafted and sent it to the addressees listed in the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my information. This information was sent to the addressees mentioned. I think that here we also don't have the cover letter, the accompanying memo saying, Hereby we submit information under such and such number also carrying my signature. However, I accept that this is my information and that it was sent to the listed recipients.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Andan --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 831D1, which is tab 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, in 1992, were you in the habit of writing notes in some sort of a diary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't really call it a diary, but, yes, I was writing down notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document bears the letters AN-6. It's in the upper left-hand corner and underlined on the first page. Could you tell me when was this document marked with those letters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can probably check this, I believe that during one of the two interviews that I had with The Hague investigators in Banja Luka and I think it was during the second interview that I gave them this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember whether it was marked AN-6 on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But in any case, Mr. Andan, these notes that you wrote pertain to the period from the end of July until the end of August, or September 1992. Could you tell me what happened to the remainder of your notes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I don't know whether it was the first or the second interview, but I offered them whatever they asked me to give them. I gave my diary in its entirety to Mr. Raffi Gregorian, the deputy high representative in Sarajevo for a number of years. I gave the diary and some other documents which were never returned to me. I was promised that all the documents that I submitted would be checked for authenticity, however, I never went back to Mr. Raffi and I never received any feedback from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you handed this diary of yours to Mr. Raffi Gregorian from the Office of the High Representative in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to him on a number of occasions. I wanted to regulate my status. Also once we spoke about an offer that Mr. Gregorian made to me on that occasion which was more or less as follows: I was supposed to find the mortal remains of Colonel Avdo Palic, and if I do that all sanctions pertaining to me would be terminated and there would be a possibly for me to return to work in the Ministry of the Interior. So it was either on that occasion or slightly before that but the crux of the matter is that I handed over my diary to him as well as some other documents. If I remember well, I also gave him a letter written by my stepfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I interject here. I'm not sure this seems to beyond the scope of what is relevant to us. I note in the proofing note that at item 14 the Defence did say they were going to have information from the witness regarding comments in relation to his diary. However, I took that to mean it was going to be comments about the content of the diary, not about some transactions or dealings with somebody of the Office of the High Representative. So I don't know where we are going here and I don't know if this is something that should be done in open session or not, but absent some further showing of how this is relevant to the issues in our case, I would ask that we not continue until that's proven to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document which I'm going to go into the content, of course that's my intention, has been received as part of the documentation which the witness provided to the Office of the Prosecutor during the interview conducted with him by the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor. However, it is apparent from the document that it is not a complete document, and I'm just establishing where is the complete document because I have never seen it, and the witness is giving the explanation where is that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think he has already said where it is. I don't know that we need any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't, but I didn't just want to stop the witness in his answer, but I'm satisfied with the answer as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I think we all are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, could you please take a look at page 3 of this document, your notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before we go to another page, can I just ask something to the witness for my information. Mr. Andan, there are three names there you that are mentioned also in the previous document, Pivarski, Niski, and Zuco, and if I understood you well, these are leaders of a group, groups of paramilitary? Are they leaders of different groups, and if so, can you give the name of the groups they were a head of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are dealing here with three different paramilitary groups. The three persons mentioned here are the respective leaders. Apart from Zuco, I cannot remember the full name of Pivarski and Niski. This here is my operative notebook. And I know that I entered information related to the presence of the paramilitary formations in Zvornik into this notebook. So besides Pivarski there are other names mentioned here, a guy named Splico and some other people. But apart from Vojin Vuckovic, because of my engagement in that particular case, I wouldn't know any other names. I only remember this one full name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I think you misunderstood me, I wanted to know Pivarski, he was a leader of which group? What was the name of the group? Same for Niski and same for Zuco, what was the name of the group they were head of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you a correct answer. I see from the notebook that Pivarski had 20 men at his disposal and he was stationed at Drinjaca, that's the Zvornik municipality. Niski had, if I can read it correctly, 30 people in the Kiseljak municipality. However, the names of the groups is something that I don't know right now. I only know that Zuco's group was called Yellow Wasps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood His Honour correctly, the question was: Was Pivarski's group a separate and distinct unit as opposed to Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, they were not part of the Yellow Wasps. There are three different paramilitary formations here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did all those three paramilitary formations, or maybe even more than three, operate, to put it that way, in the territory of the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from my notebook that they separated among themselves, divided the territory into their zones of responsibility, if I can put it that way. Zuco took the town of Zvornik; Pivarski, the settlement of Drinjaca; while Niski held Kiseljak, the settlement of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The settlement of Drinjaca and the settlement of Kiseljak, are they also part of the town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that all belongs to the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm looking at your notebook and I can see the entry saying Simo Chetnik, it's the fourth line, could you please read out what it says for Simo Chetnik and could you explain it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the fourth paramilitary formation led by one Simo Chetnik. He had 30 men and he was controlling the Malesevic area. That's what it says in my notebook, and that is also a part of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last entry on this page, can you read that out loud?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where I noted the disposition of Zuco's forces. Part of the forces belonging to the Zuco's unit was in a skyscraper called Soliter, on the sixth floor. They had taken over the whole of the sixth floor. Then, after that, it's a private house across the street from the hotel, that's where they used to get together. Then the third line, this is my observation, that they monitor and control the whole town. I already told you that they monitored not only simple civilians but also local dignitaries, people who were part of the local authorities at the time and not only them but also some of our operatives who were tasked with their surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in Serbian, we have the correct page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to explain the following entry. Is it something to do with the weaponry that the Yellow Wasps had at the time according to your information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and a number of other operatives during our stay in Zvornik learned that the part of the unit was accommodated in Zvornik in the Glinica factory. We learned that they were building some sort of an armoured train. They invested a fantastic 1 million euros into equipping of this train in order to use the train for a break-through towards Kalesija so that the town of Kalesija could be taken over. At the time Kalesija was under the control of the BiH army. So this is just a short list of what was in that train and the equipment that was there. You can see towards the end that they attempted an action with the train between Caparde and Celopek, that those are two points in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, it is the time we take the adjournment for the week. We resume at 9.00 on Monday morning. I believe we are in Courtroom I. So I trust everyone has a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 30th day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.
